strengths.title: Parameterized data access throughout
strengths.detail: EF Core LINQ only. Zero FromSqlRaw / ExecuteSqlRaw / string-concatenated SQL across 148 files. The four 'SQL' string matches in D4DemoService.cs are documentation strings, not executed statements.

strengths.title: No XSS sinks
strengths.detail: Zero MarkupString or Html.Raw usages; Blazor's automatic contextual encoding is intact on every render path.

strengths.title: No hard-coded secrets
strengths.detail: No credentials, API keys or private key material in source or configuration. The connection string is a local file path with no password.

strengths.title: Transport and header baseline in place
strengths.detail: HTTPS redirection, HSTS, antiforgery, rate limiting, and SecurityHeadersMiddleware setting nosniff, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy.

strengths.title: Seed-file I/O uses a fixed server path
strengths.detail: No user input reaches a filesystem path; no traversal exposure in the seeding routine.

findings.title: No authentication or authorization anywhere in the application
findings.evidence: 0 [Authorize] attributes across 148 files. No AddAuthentication, AddAuthorization, UseAuthentication or UseAuthorization calls in Program.cs. MapBlazorHub() is mapped with no RequireAuthorization().
findings.risk: Any anonymous visitor who can reach the URL can read and modify every customer, order and stock record, and can open a SignalR circuit to invoke server-side component logic directly.

remediation.summary: Register an identity provider and apply a global default-deny authorization policy, so every page requires sign-in without editing any page.
steps: Add ASP.NET Core Identity or the organisation's OIDC provider: AddAuthentication().AddOpenIdConnect(...) plus AddAuthorization().
Call UseAuthentication() and UseAuthorization() before UseAntiforgery() in the middleware pipeline.
Set a global fallback policy - AddAuthorizationBuilder().SetFallbackPolicy(new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder().RequireAuthenticatedUser().Build()) - so new pages are protected by default.
Mark the sign-in, health and error endpoints [AllowAnonymous].
Protect the circuit: app.MapBlazorHub().RequireAuthorization().

findings.verification: An unauthenticated GET /customers returns 302 to the sign-in endpoint. After signing in, /customers renders exactly as it does today. dotnet build reports 0 errors and the seeded data still displays.

findings.title: IDOR - record routes return any record by id with no ownership check
findings.evidence: Both detail routes bind an integer id straight from the URL and load the record with no ownership, role or tenant predicate. Incrementing the id walks the whole table.
findings.risk: Enumeration of the full customer and order tables by anyone who can reach the app - names, addresses, phone numbers and order history.

remediation.summary: Authentication (S-1) closes anonymous enumeration. For a multi-tenant deployment, additionally scope the load query to the caller.
steps: Apply S-1 first - it removes anonymous access to these routes entirely.
If the application is or will become multi-tenant, add the ownership predicate to the query itself rather than checking after loading, so a missing check fails closed.
For a single-tenant back-office application, authentication plus the S-3 write role is sufficient; record that decision in the threat model.
remediation.codeAfter:
var customer = await _service.get_customerAsync(CustomerNum, currentUser.TenantId);
// query filters on TenantId - a forgotten check returns null, not another tenant's row

findings.verification: An authenticated user can open records belonging to their tenant; a request for another tenant's id returns 404, not the record. An anonymous request is redirected to sign-in.

findings.title: Content Security Policy allows unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval in script-src
findings.evidence: script-src permits both 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval', which removes most of the policy's value as an XSS mitigation.
findings.risk: Defense-in-depth failure. There is no XSS sink today (see strengths), but if one is introduced, CSP will not stop the injected script from executing.

remediation.summary: Drop unsafe-eval, then replace unsafe-inline for scripts with a per-request nonce. Stage the change through report-only mode so it cannot break the app silently.
steps: Remove 'unsafe-eval' - Blazor Server does not require it. Nothing should break.
Deploy the tightened policy as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only for one release and review the violation reports.
Replace 'unsafe-inline' for scripts with a per-request nonce and add that nonce to the framework script tags in _Layout.cshtml.
Keep style-src 'unsafe-inline' - MudBlazor requires it, and style injection is materially lower risk than script injection.

findings.verification: The app loads and is fully interactive under the tightened policy, and the browser console shows zero CSP violations across the main routes.

findings.title: No server-side input validation on any DTO or edit model

locations.excerpt: public string Fname { get; set; } = string.Empty;

findings.evidence: Zero DataAnnotations attributes and no FluentValidation validators across the DTO and edit-model types. The EditForm has no <DataAnnotationsValidator/>.
findings.risk: The legacy 4GL screen enforced field widths at the terminal. Over HTTP that constraint no longer exists, so over-length and malformed values now reach the data layer directly - a textbook migration-exposed gap.

remediation.summary: Add DataAnnotations matching the real column widths from the schema, and a DataAnnotationsValidator to each EditForm.
steps: Read the real column lengths from the schema - Fname 15, Lname 15, State 2, Zipcode 5 - and mirror them exactly. Do not invent stricter limits: rejecting values the system previously accepted would be a behaviour change.
Add [Required], [StringLength], [Range] and [RegularExpression] to the edit models accordingly.
Add <DataAnnotationsValidator /> and a <ValidationSummary /> to each EditForm.
Keep validation server-side; the Blazor Server model already evaluates it on the server.
remediation.codeBefore:
public string Fname { get; set; } = string.Empty;
public string State { get; set; } = string.Empty;

findings.verification: A 200-character first name is rejected with a validation message; a 14-character name saves normally and the record is unchanged in shape.

findings.title: Customer PII stored unencrypted at rest
findings.evidence: The SQLite database file holds customer names, addresses and phone numbers as plaintext. Any read access to the filesystem or any backup copy exposes the full dataset.
findings.risk: A stolen backup, a misconfigured volume mount or filesystem access through another flaw yields the entire customer table with no further effort.

remediation.summary: Encrypt at the storage layer - SQLCipher or an encrypted volume - keeping the key in a secret store. Prefer platform encryption over column encryption so queries are unaffected.
steps: Switch to the SQLCipher-backed SQLite provider and supply the key through configuration: Data Source=stores7.db;Password=<from secret store>.
Store the key in user-secrets for development and Key Vault / Secrets Manager in production - never in appsettings.json.
Alternatively, host the file on an encrypted volume if the platform provides one; this needs no code change at all.
Do not use column-level encryption here - it would break sorting and filtering on the affected columns.
remediation.verificationNote: Queries and indexes are unchanged under storage-layer encryption.

findings.verification: The .db file is not readable as plaintext with a hex viewer or the sqlite3 CLI without the key; the application opens it with the key and every page behaves as before.

findings.title: Deprecated X-XSS-Protection header is set
findings.evidence: The header is set on every response. Modern browsers ignore it, and its legacy auditor could itself introduce vulnerabilities in older engines.
findings.risk: No direct exploitability. It is noise that suggests the header set has not been reviewed recently.

remediation.summary: Remove the header. CSP (S-4) is the modern control for this class of attack.
steps: Delete the X-XSS-Protection line from SecurityHeadersMiddleware.

findings.verification: The header is absent from responses; no behaviour change anywhere in the app.

findings.title: No automated dependency vulnerability scanning in the pipeline
findings.evidence: Declared packages: MudBlazor 8.0.0, Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite 10.0.0, QuestPDF 2024.12.0, Serilog.AspNetCore 9.0.0, SQLitePCLRaw 3.0.4. No CI step runs a vulnerability check. This audit had no advisory source available, so the packages were NOT checked against a vulnerability database - their status is unknown, not clean.
findings.risk: A vulnerable dependency would go unnoticed until it was exploited. This is a continuous risk, not a point-in-time one - a package that is clean today may have an advisory published tomorrow.

remediation.summary: Add a dependency vulnerability gate to CI and fail the build on High or Critical advisories.
steps: Add 'dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive' as a CI step and fail on High/Critical.
Enable Dependabot or Renovate so upgrade PRs are raised automatically.
Run the check once now, out of band, to establish the current position - this audit could not.
remediation.codeAfter:
- name: Dependency vulnerability check
  run: |
    dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive 2>&1 | tee vuln.txt
    ! grep -qE 'High|Critical' vuln.txt

findings.verification: The CI step runs on every build and is green; deliberately pinning a known-vulnerable package version turns it red.

roadmap.name: Access control
roadmap.rationale: The largest single risk reduction available. S-1 subsumes most of S-2: once the global policy is in place, anonymous enumeration is gone, and only the multi-tenant scoping remains.

roadmap.name: Configuration hardening
roadmap.rationale: Hours of work for real points. The report-only soak in S-4 means the CSP change carries no deployment risk.

roadmap.name: Data and input
roadmap.rationale: Closes the two gaps the migration exposed: the terminal no longer constrains field widths, and the data file is no longer on a controlled host.

roadmap.name: Operational
roadmap.rationale: Makes the dependency position continuously visible rather than a point-in-time unknown.

evidenceLog.result: 0 executed matches; 4 documentation strings in D4DemoService.cs

evidenceLog.conclusion: Baseline present; CSP weak - Finding S-4

evidenceLog.result: 5 direct packages inventoried; NO advisory database reachable

cost.note: Measured from the session transcript; assistant messages deduplicated by message id. List rates only - excludes enterprise discounts, Batch API pricing and partner-platform rates.

limitations: Static analysis only. The application was not built, deployed, or exercised at runtime, so no finding here reflects observed behaviour.

Dependency advisories were NOT verified against a live vulnerability database - no advisory MCP server was configured and no network access was used. The dependency position is unknown, not clean. See S-9.
Infrastructure, network policy, WAF rules, reverse-proxy configuration and deployed secrets were out of scope; only files under the target path were examined.

The Informix 4GL source was not audited in this run (meta.migration.sourcePathAudited is null), so 'legacy-inherited' vs 'migration-introduced' classifications are inferred from the generated code alone.
Business-logic correctness was assessed only where intent was inferable from the code. Domain rules such as valid state transitions and pricing authority were not verified.
2,104 files were skipped as build output, minified web assets or binaries.
